LEHRP · Water Pathway Audit · September 2026

The Purple-Pipe Loop

Ladera Ranch's drainage is captured at the Horno Basin and re-sprayed on the community through the purple-pipe recycled-water system. This report maps that loop from official sources and aerial imagery, then audits a community-raised theory: that pesticides, pharmaceuticals, and untested legacy arsenic could recirculate and compound in it.

Read this first. This is an independent research and data-organization project. It does not provide medical advice and does not establish that any party caused any illness. No contaminant is asserted to be present in any water or soil discussed here; the relevant streams have not been publicly tested for the constituents examined, which is itself a central finding. Every claim carries a statement class (verified fact, official statement, scientific finding, model estimate, inference, hypothesis, missing evidence). Geographic and temporal overlap does not establish exposure or causation.

1 · The loop is real — verified

The water district's own materials establish the geometry A2:

» The district "collects urban return (runoff) water from Oso Creek, Dove Creek, and Horno Creek to blend with the recycled water as an additional source for irrigation." (District recycled-water page.)

» The "Horno Basin... designed to capture, treat and deliver millions of gallons of runoff water for local irrigation use." (District newsletter, May 2012, archived with hash.)

The delivery network is the community's purple-pipe system — the lavender-colored piping that industry-wide marks recycled, non-potable water. It irrigates the slopes, parks, medians, and common-area turf of Ladera Ranch. So water that drains off the community's landscapes is captured at the bottom of the watershed and a portion of it is sprayed back onto those same landscapes. That is not a theory; it is the design intent, stated by its operator.

1b · The route, step by step — resolved from the regulatory record A2 · updated Sep 11

The governing document is the San Diego Regional Water Quality Control Board's Addendum No. 4 to Order No. 97-52 (adopted October 8, 2008; archived in this project with SHA-256 hash A2). It permits the Horno Urban Water Recovery Facility by name, at the southern end of Ladera Ranch (Tract 15793, Horno Creek Hydrologic Subarea 901.27, San Juan Creek watershed). Combining the permit with the district's program descriptions, the water's full circuit is:

1 — Streets to creek. Dry-weather runoff from Ladera's roofs, lawns, streets and slopes enters the storm system and the vegetated Sienna Botanica corridor (~2.4 miles along Sienna Parkway) and drains to Horno Creek, the community's trunk drainage.

2 — Creek to basin. At the bottom of the watershed the flow collects in the Horno Water Quality Basin — owned and operated by the County of Orange. (Storm flows exceeding the basin's dry-weather capture continue downstream toward San Juan Creek and the ocean; the loop diverts the low flows.)

3 — Basin to wetlands. Diverted water passes "through seven acres of constructed wetlands, owned by Ladera Ranch Homeowners Association" — vegetated treatment for sediment and nutrients. This is the entire engineered treatment train for the captured stream.

4 — Wetlands to the purple pipes. From the wetlands the water is pumped into the district's recycled water distribution system — the permit's words: "prior to blending with recycled water" for "subsequent landscape irrigation use." The blend joins recycled water already in the distribution network.

5 — Storage and pressure. The non-potable distribution system is fed and pressurized from its storage — the ridge tanks (the pair "up top" with the larger third) serve the local pressure zones. The exact pipe alignment and blend point are the one detail still held only in the engineer-of-record as-builts; the destination is documented.

6 — Sprinklers to soil, and around again. The blend is sprayed on Ladera's slopes, parks, medians and common-area turf — about 180 acre-feet (~59 million gallons) per dry season. Water evaporates or soaks in; the next runoff heads back down Horno Creek.

1c · Why the water does NOT filter through Chiquita — the proof A2

Four independent lines of evidence from the permit and district record establish that the captured runoff bypasses the Chiquita Water Reclamation Plant:

Proof 1 — the permit's stated sequence names no plant. The route is given as basin → wetlands → blend → irrigation. A treatment plant is nowhere in the described train. If runoff entered Chiquita's process, it would become recycled water; instead the permit consistently treats "diversion water" as a distinct stream that merely blends with recycled water.

Proof 2 — the monitoring provisions only make sense if the streams are separate. Provision K.1 requires sampling of "diversion water either prior to, or after mixing with, recycled water." Provision K.2 requires sampling of "effluent from the recycled water facilities at the point of discharge, prior to blending with diversion water." Regulators wrote two monitoring points for two different streams that meet downstream of the plant's discharge. That language is incoherent if the runoff passed through the plant.

Proof 3 — the waived parameters are sewage-plant parameters. K.1 exempts the diversion water from Biochemical Oxygen Demand, Total Suspended Solids, and Odor limits — the classic wastewater-treatment metrics. The exemption exists precisely because this stream is not plant effluent and was never processed as sewage.

Proof 4 — the program design is direct-to-distribution. The district's own description of its sibling facility (the Upper Oso Barrier) is that it "collects runoff and delivers... recycled water for irrigation use" — capture-and-deliver, not capture-and-treat-at-plant. Geography agrees: the basin sits at Ladera's low point and the plant is across the open space up Chiquita Canyon; the permitted design pumps to the distribution system, not across the canyon and back.

Net: the captured runoff receives basin settling and wetland treatment only — no tertiary treatment, no plant processes — before it is sprayed on the community. That is not an accusation; it is the permitted design, and it is typical for urban-runoff recovery. What makes it significant here is the untested legacy of the land it drains.

2 · The audit — what fails, what survives

The theory as raised: constituents "build up" because the basin "does not treat for those chemicals," making "one big ongoing toxic loop that compounds." We stress-tested each clause.

FAILS AUDIT — "compounds" in the water. The loop is partial, not closed. Storm flows bypass the capture (dry-weather diversions take low flows only); evapotranspiration removes water; irrigation blends captured runoff into a much larger recycled+imported supply; some water infiltrates. A steady-state recirculation model Model estimate caps water-phase enrichment even under generous assumptions:

ScenarioRunoff fraction fCapture cPass-through rWater multiplier
Conservative0.080.400.50×1.02
Moderate0.150.600.70×1.07
Aggressive upper bound0.300.800.90×1.28
Fully closed loop (impossible)0.501.001.00×2.00

Runaway concentration in the water supply is not physically supported. Reporting otherwise would be sensationalism, and it would be wrong.

SURVIVES AUDIT — redistribution. The loop's real significance is geographic: whatever the drainage carries — dissolved or fine-particulate — gets pumped back uphill and sprayed across every purple-pipe-irrigated surface in the community. A constituent that started in one place ends up everywhere the sprinklers reach. Inference from verified geometry

SURVIVES AUDIT — accumulation in soil. Irrigation water evaporates; persistent constituents do not. Metals (arsenic among them) and persistent pesticide residues left behind by each cycle accumulate in landscape soils roughly linearly with years of application — independent of the loop's water-phase gain. Two-plus decades of purple-pipe irrigation is two-plus decades of deposition. Magnitude: unmeasured. Scientific principle + missing evidence

SURVIVES AUDIT — the treatment gap, as an open question. Basin-level urban-runoff facilities of this type are engineered for trash, sediment, and gross solids; dissolved metals and dissolved organics largely pass filtration B1 — general engineering literature. Tertiary treatment at the Chiquita plant (Title 22) removes pathogens and solids and only partially removes pharmaceuticals and other trace organics B1. Whether THIS basin's works remove any dissolved constituent is documented in the engineer-of-record drawings and the district's permit file — both obtainable by public-records request, neither yet in hand. Missing evidence

3 · The chemicals, taken one at a time

ConstituentEnters the loop howEvidence status
Landscape pesticides (fipronil, pyrethroids)Applied on HOA/residential landscaping; wash off in irrigation runoff — the classic Southern California urban-runoff signalPresence in regional urban runoff: B1. Levels in THIS loop: untested
Pharmaceuticals / trace organicsSurvive tertiary treatment in part; enter via the recycled-water blendPhenomenon: B1. Levels in this blend: not publicly reported
Arsenic (legacy, 1907–1912 era)IF present in drainage soils (unmeasured), mobilizes in runoff as dissolved and fine-particulate phases; filtration does not remove the dissolved phaseHypothesis — no soil or runoff arsenic data exists for this watershed; the historical program on this land is documented A1

On "never tested": the district's drinking water is tested and reports arsenic at non-detect to trace levels — that system is separate and not at issue here. What has no public testing record is the captured-runoff stream, the basin sediment, and the irrigated landscape soils — the loop itself. That gap is the finding.

4 · The endpoints, from the air

VERDICT ON THE THEORY

Not supported as stated: "one big ongoing toxic loop that compounds" — the water-phase compounding fails a straightforward mass-balance audit, and honesty about that is what keeps the rest credible.

Supported, restated defensibly: Ladera Ranch operates a documented capture-and-respray loop through its purple-pipe system. That loop redistributes whatever the community's drainage carries onto its landscapes, deposits persistent constituents into landscape soils year after year, and does so with no public monitoring of the captured-runoff stream for pesticides, pharmaceuticals, or legacy arsenic — on land where a federal arsenical dipping program operated a century ago and where soil has never been tested for it. Update, Sept 11: the route is resolved from the Regional Board record — county basin → HOA wetlands → blended into the purple pipes, bypassing the treatment plant; permit-era sampling covered salts and nutrients only. The reported pattern warrants investigation; the current data are insufficient to determine whether any constituent is present at levels of concern.

Conclusions, in the project's language discipline:

C1 (verified). Ladera Ranch's dry-weather drainage is captured at the bottom of its watershed and returned to the community as landscape irrigation through the purple-pipe system — a designed, permitted, operating loop of roughly 59 million gallons per dry season.

C2 (verified). The returned water's entire treatment consists of a county-owned settling basin and seven acres of HOA-owned constructed wetlands. It does not pass through the Chiquita Water Reclamation Plant; tertiary treatment is not part of this stream's train.

C3 (verified as a records gap). Neither the permit's characterization sampling, its ongoing monitoring scheme as written in the addendum, nor any environmental review analyzed this stream for arsenic, pesticides, or pharmaceuticals. Twenty years of operation, no public toxics data.

C4 (model + inference). The loop cannot make the water itself "compound" toxic — the physics caps water-phase enrichment. Its significance is redistribution (whatever the drainage carries is sprayed community-wide) and deposition (evaporation leaves persistent constituents in landscape soils, accumulating year over year).

C5 (hypothesis, testable). On land with a documented 1907–1912 arsenical dipping history and no soil testing, the loop constitutes a plausible, unexamined redistribution pathway. Whether it carries anything of concern is unknown — and knowable for the cost of four samples, starting with a jar of water from a purple-pipe sprinkler head.

The current data are insufficient to determine whether any constituent is present at levels of concern; the reported pattern and the documented records gap warrant the measurements described above.
